prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Britain's Prince William has helped the U.S. Coast Guard bust a drug smuggling boat carrying cocaine worth a minimum of $80 million. Prince William has helped bust a speed boat smuggling $80 million worth of cocaine. William, who is serving in the Royal Navy, helped make the bust last weekend when he spotted a speedboat found to be carrying nearly a ton of cocaine in the Atlantic Ocean, Britain's Ministry of Defense said Wednesday. William, 26, was one of the crew members aboard a helicopter attached to the frigate HMS Iron Duke who spotted the ocean-going speedboat hundreds of miles northeast of Barbados, the defense ministry said . The 50-foot-long power boat raised suspicions because it was a small vessel far out to sea and resembled a "go-fast" boat commonly used for drug smuggling, the ministry said. The boat's location suggested it was en route to Europe or North Africa, it said. The chopper's crew informed the ship's captain about the boat, and U.S. Coast Guard personnel who were on the frigate then boarded the boat. They found 45 bales of cocaine weighing a total of 900 kilograms (just under a ton), the defense ministry said. The cocaine has a minimum street value of $80 million, the ministry said. The bust went smoothly with no violence, defense officials said. Navy crew detained the five men on the boat, which was in poor condition and later sank. William is in the middle of a two-month attachment with the Royal Navy as part of his continued experience with various branches of the military. The prince, who is called sub lieutenant Wales in the navy, is also expected to spend time aboard a mine hunter and submarine during his attachment, which ends August 1. William's vessel, the Iron Duke, is a patrol boat which supports overseas British territories in the event of a hurricane and carries out counter-narcotic operations. William completed a four-month attachment with the Royal Air Force earlier this year and received his pilot's wings on graduation in April. He learned to fly three different aircraft during the attachment and is known as Flying Officer Wales within the RAF. William is already a second lieutenant in the British Army, where he serves in the Blues and Royals regiment of the Household Cavalry. The attachments are designed to give the prince, who as king will be the head of the armed forces, experience with the military.

William, then a 26-year-old Royal Navy sub-lieutenant, was serving aboard the frigate HMS *Iron Duke* when its crew targeted the suspected smuggling vessel in 2008.

A US Coast Guard law-enforcement detachment operating from the British ship boarded the speedboat and discovered roughly 900 kilograms — nearly one ton — of cocaine. At the time, officials estimated the drugs were worth at least $80 million.

The prince was involved in the surveillance and coordination that led to the interception, according to reports of the operation. He did not personally board the suspected smuggling boat.

The seizure came as HMS *Iron Duke* conducted counter-narcotics patrols in cooperation with US authorities, part of a broader effort to disrupt trafficking routes through the Caribbean.

William’s attachment to the Royal Navy was one stage of his military career. He later served as a search-and-rescue helicopter pilot with the Royal Air Force and subsequently as an air-ambulance pilot.

## Prince William’s role in the Atlantic drugs operation

In June 2008, Prince William took part in a Royal Navy counter-narcotics patrol while serving aboard the frigate **HMS *Iron Duke*** in the Caribbean and western Atlantic. Operating under the service name **Sub-Lieutenant Wales**, he was integrated into the ship’s crew and assisted with the operation, although officials did not disclose his precise duties. He did **not personally board the smugglers’ vessel**.

### The seizure

- *Iron Duke*’s **Lynx helicopter** detected and pursued a suspicious high-speed “go-fast” boat near Barbados.
- Those aboard began throwing packages into the sea as they fled.
- The Navy recovered **45 bales containing about 900 kilograms—nearly one metric ton—of cocaine**.
- British authorities estimated the drugs’ street value at approximately **£40 million**.
- The operation formed part of a wider, internationally coordinated effort against cocaine trafficking through the Caribbean and Atlantic.

### The suspects

The suspected traffickers escaped in the speedboat after reaching waters where the Royal Navy could not continue the pursuit. Consequently, **no suspects were arrested during that interception**. Contemporary accounts did not publicly identify those aboard.

### William’s military training

The deployment was part of William’s **five-week Royal Navy attachment**, intended to give the future senior royal practical experience in each branch of Britain’s armed forces. Before joining *Iron Duke*, he had:

- Graduated from the **Royal Military Academy Sandhurst**;
- Been commissioned as an Army officer in the **Blues and Royals**, part of the Household Cavalry;
- Undertaken an attachment with the **Royal Air Force**, including pilot training.

His naval program included shipboard watchkeeping, navigation and other routine operational duties. The counter-drug mission therefore gave him direct exposure to a real Royal Navy maritime-security operation rather than being solely a ceremonial deployment.

# Prince William Helps Bust $80 Million Cocaine Smuggling Boat

**BRIDGETOWN, Barbados —** Prince William took part in a Royal Navy operation that led to the seizure of nearly 900 kilograms of cocaine from a speedboat in the Caribbean, British defense officials said, in a haul valued at about $80 million at the time.

The operation occurred in 2008 while the prince, then 26 and second in line to the British throne, was completing a naval attachment aboard the frigate HMS *Iron Duke*. The warship was conducting counter-narcotics patrols in cooperation with regional authorities and a United States Coast Guard law-enforcement team.

The suspect vessel was detected in waters northeast of Barbados during a coordinated surveillance mission. HMS *Iron Duke* moved to intercept the boat, while the embarked Coast Guard personnel carried out the law-enforcement phase of the operation. Several people aboard the vessel were detained, and officers discovered dozens of packages containing cocaine.

British officials estimated the shipment’s wholesale value at approximately £40 million—roughly $80 million under exchange rates prevailing at the time. The seizure removed a substantial quantity of narcotics believed to have been destined for international markets.

Prince William participated as a junior naval officer and member of the ship’s company. His duties included supporting surveillance and operational activities, though officials did not suggest that he personally boarded the suspected smuggling vessel or made arrests.

The mission formed part of his broader familiarization training with Britain’s armed services. William, who had already served with the British Army and later trained as a Royal Air Force search-and-rescue pilot, spent several weeks aboard HMS *Iron Duke* to gain experience of Royal Navy operations.

The Caribbean is a major transit corridor for cocaine produced in South America and moved toward North America and Europe. Naval patrols in the region frequently combine military surveillance capabilities with civilian or Coast Guard officers authorized to board vessels, conduct searches and make arrests.

HMS *Iron Duke*, a Type 23 frigate, was deployed to the region for maritime-security duties that included counter-smuggling operations, disaster-relief readiness and support for British overseas territories. Its helicopters, radar systems and high-speed boats allowed it to monitor large areas and respond rapidly to suspicious vessels.

The seizure attracted international attention because of the prince’s presence, but defense officials emphasized that it was a joint operation involving the frigate’s full crew and specialist American law-enforcement personnel.

The episode became one of the most prominent operational moments of William’s early military career, illustrating both the international nature of Caribbean counter-narcotics work and the Royal Navy’s role in disrupting maritime trafficking routes.
